description: I’m an engineer working in the tech industry and have always been a tech girl at heart. While technology has always been my world, I’ve also been fascinated by galaxies, space, and the mysteries of the universe. I’ve always wanted to learn more about how the universe works and understand the natural phenomena happening beyond our planet.
summary:
Last Transmissions is an interactive web experience by Soomal Qureshi that gives a voice to the robots NASA has left across the solar system. Children tap one of 12 machines on the Moon, on Mars or in deep space, including Surveyor 3, the Lunar Rover, Viking 1, Sojourner, Spirit, Opportunity, InSight, Ingenuity, Pioneer 10, Voyager 1 and New Horizons. Each one tells its own story in the first person, in very simple words. Every card has a cartoon portrait, a description of what the real hardware looks like, “How I worked”, “What I discovered”, a status badge (silent, still working or still travelling) and audio narration. A quiz and a “Which explorer are you?” game help the facts stick.

It addresses the challenge by turning dense mission history into a story that links the engineering to the science, for school-age and casual space fans. It matters because most young people only hear about active missions. These machines show how past exploration made today’s discoveries possible.
details:
Last Transmissions (Team AstroGeeks, by Soomal Qureshi)

What it does and how it works: Last Transmissions is an interactive website that lets children meet 12 pieces of NASA hardware left on the Moon, on Mars and in deep space. A visitor picks a place, taps a machine, and it tells its own story . Each card has a cartoon portrait, a plain description of what the real hardware looks like, “How I worked”, “What I discovered”, a status badge (silent, still working or still travelling) and audio narration read aloud by a female voice. A mission quiz and a “Which explorer are you?” game help the facts stick.

Benefits: It turns dense mission history into short, simple stories that link engineering to science. It needs no account, no downloads and no payment, and it works as one self-contained page.

Intended impact: Most young people only hear about current missions. This project shows that older machines, such as Surveyor 3, Viking 1, Opportunity and Pioneer 10, made today’s exploration possible, and it invites children to feel a personal connection to them and to ask questions about space.

Tools and technology: The site is a single file written in HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with no outside libraries. The cartoon scenes are drawn as inline SVG graphics, and the starfield is drawn on an HTML canvas. Narration uses the browser’s built-in Web Speech feature, and the optional ambient space sound is generated live with the Web Audio feature. It is hosted as a free, public static page. The demo slides were made in PowerPoint and shared through Google Drive in pdf.

Creativity: The robots are the narrators. Each one is a character with a face and a voice, written like a diary of its mission, so children are not reading a fact sheet. The page has a nebula sky, an orbiting mini solar system, shooting stars and drifting planets, and the “Which explorer are you?” game lets children find the robot that matches their personality.

Factors we considered: Audience: ages 9–14, with very simple words and short sentences. Accuracy and timeliness: mission details are based on NASA mission information, and the statuses of Voyager 1 (one light-day from Earth on November 18, 2026) and New Horizons (awake in 2026) are current. Accessibility: audio narration, keyboard-friendly buttons, and motion that stops for visitors who prefer less movement. Safety and privacy: no ads, tracking or sign-ups. Copyright: we used original cartoon art and give links to real NASA photos instead of copying them.
